newsitem.title: USA: U.S. debt futures finish lower, led by T-bonds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. debt futures finish lower, led by T-bonds.

text.p: U.S. debt futures finished lower, with the losses in the T-bond market dominating market activity in the latter half of trade, traders said.
They said hedge funds, leveraged funds and portfolio managers, who were lightening up positions, were aggressive sellers in the T-bond futures pit.
About 50,000, or roughly $5 billion worth of T-bond futures were sold in the afternoon, and about 40,000, or $4 billion, 10-year note futures were sold by funds in the afternoon.
March slipped to 112-24/32, raising the possibility that the market will soon re-test Friday's pit low of 112-22/32.
The contract would have to retrace its losses to 113-21/32 at the least in order to reverse the bearish trend, traders and analysts said.
March T-bonds, however, could barely rise to 113-07/32 on Wednesday afternoon, some noted.
Meanwhile, Eurodollars stabilized at lower levels, reflecting the slight steepening of the cash two- to 30-year yield curve, traders said.
June Eurodollars are not expected to fall below support at 94.24. A breach of 94.24 would take the contract no lower than 94.22 to the October 4 settlement of 94.21, traders said.
Traders said concerns about a decline in U.S. stock prices led to some flight-to-quality in short-term debt instruments.
Growing expectations for a correction in U.S. equities has been the main focus of the U.S. bond futures market.

While traders acknowledged the Wall Street Journal article on the possibility of Japanese investors limiting exposure in U.S. Treasuries, they said there was little cited in the article to put those worries back on the front-burner.
"The fact that "some traders" believe this should not cause the bond market to panic," Brian Wesbury, chief economist at Griffin, Kubik, Stephens & Thompson, Inc, said.
Wesbury, who wrote his comments in a newsletter, attributed losses in U.S. asset markets to Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's comments last week.
March bonds' one-month low of 112-08/32 was set on Friday's GLOBEX session in reaction to Greenspan's warnings of "irrational exuberance" in asset markets.

"The obvious conclusion is that the Fed might not ease if the stock market were high, because lower interest rates would push stocks even higher," Wesbury wrote. As a result, Wesbury said the economic data that is usually so key to the markets' direction will have less affect on prices this week.

Traders quickly assessed the U.S. November Producer Price Index (PPI) as a "wash," and spoke little about Thursday's slate of U.S. economic reports, like the Consumer Price Index (CPI). CPI is forecast to rise 0.3 percent, from up 0.3 percent in October, while the core rate is seen gaining 0.2 percent, also unchanged from October.

At the end of pit trade, March bonds were off 1-15/32 at 112-29/32, 10-year notes fell 1-00 at 109-16/32, June T-bills were off three bps at 94.89, March Eurodollars were down four bps at 94.44 and June Eurodollars were off seven bps at 94.30.
